lead: Every MOSFET terminal pair is a small capacitor, and every cycle the driving gate charges and discharges these capacitors through series resistances. The gate oxide gives the largest part, but overlap and junction capacitances add to it, and their split among source, drain, gate and bulk changes with the operating region. These parasitics set switching delay, dynamic power and fan-out. Cell libraries and SPICE models carry them as Cox, overlap and junction parameters. The same numbers explain why a wide driver is fast and why a minimum-size transistor still has input capacitance.
prereq: You need: 1.1 for the channel and 1.2 for the region boundary at V_T.

blocks.text: The gate and the channel form a parallel-plate capacitor. The insulator is the gate oxide. Its capacitance per unit area is:

blocks.where: Cox is oxide capacitance per unit area in F/m²; εox is the permittivity of silicon dioxide, about 3.45×10⁻¹¹ F/m; tox is oxide thickness in m.

blocks.text: For a transistor of width W and length L, the gate area capacitance is CoxWL. Define W as the distance across the channel, perpendicular to current, and L as the channel length from source to drain. Use consistent units: Cox in fF/µm² with W and L in µm gives capacitance in fF.
Real source and drain diffusions spread a little under the gate. This lateral diffusion creates overlap capacitance. SPICE stores it per unit width:
Cgs,ov = CGSO · W,   Cgd,ov = CGDO · W,   Cgb,ov = CGBO · W
blocks.where: CGSO, CGDO and CGBO are overlap capacitances per unit width in F/m; W is width in m. Write Cov for the overlap capacitance per side; Cov = CGSO·W = CGDO·W when the two sides match.

blocks.text: CGSO and CGDO grow when the lateral diffusion is large relative to L. In a short-channel device the overlap part can exceed the ideal area part. Fringing fields from the gate to source and drain are often folded into these same parameters by the model.

sections.h3: The Meyer model: splitting the gate capacitance

blocks.text: The gate capacitance is not always connected the same way. The Meyer model splits the gate charge among source, drain and bulk according to the region. The inversion channel is the moving plate. The figure above lists the split for the worked device.

In cutoff there is no inversion channel. The gate sees only the overlap capacitances to source and drain, and the area capacitance goes to bulk through the depleted silicon: Cgs = Cgd = Cov and Cgb ≈ CoxWL. In the linear region the channel is a resistor connecting source and drain. The gate capacitance divides equally: Cgs = Cgd ≈ ½CoxWL + Cov and Cgb = 0. In saturation the channel is pinched off near the drain. Most of the gate charge is reached from the source: Cgs ≈ ⅔CoxWL + Cov, Cgd ≈ Cov and Cgb = 0.

The fractions ½ and ⅔ are approximations. They come from integrating the channel charge along the channel. Use them for hand estimates. A simulator uses a smoother model near the boundaries, but the three cases give the right intuition.

The sum changes with region. In saturation the gate capacitance seen by the driver is Cgs + Cgd, not CoxWL. A transistor driven into saturation presents less capacitance than its area suggests, while the same transistor in cutoff presents almost none to the source but the full area to the bulk.
Source and drain diffusions form pn junctions with the bulk. Each junction has two parts: a bottom area and a sidewall perimeter. SPICE uses:

blocks.where: Cj0 is zero-bias capacitance per unit area in F/m²; V is reverse bias across the junction in V, positive for reverse bias; VB is built-in potential in V; m is the grading coefficient, about 0.3 to 0.5.

blocks.text: The area part is CJ × area. The sidewall part is CJSW × perimeter. CJ and CJSW are per unit area and per unit length. Both are voltage dependent. As V rises, Cj falls. For a source at the same potential as the bulk, V is small and the capacitance is near Cj0. For a drain that swings, the capacitance changes during the cycle.

Series resistance comes from three places. The source and drain diffusion have sheet resistance, so a long diffusion acts as a resistor. The contacts add fixed contact resistance. The polysilicon gate is a distributed resistor: the gate contact charges the channel through a resistive strip. For a wide device, model the gate as an RC ladder, not one resistor. These resistances slow charging even when the capacitance is small. In a short-channel device, source/drain resistance can be a significant fraction of the channel resistance.
Use the parasitic values from the technology file. Never guess them from W and L alone when a layout is available.

figure.caption: Rows give gate-source, gate-drain and gate-bulk capacitance in femtofarads for the worked device. Notice that bulk takes the full area capacitance only in cutoff, and source takes most of it in saturation.

spec.title: Gate capacitance by region: Cgs, Cgd, Cgb (fF)
spec.aria: A three-row table giving gate-source, gate-drain and gate-bulk capacitance in cutoff, linear and saturation, with the bulk taking the full oxide capacitance only in cutoff and the source taking most of it in saturation.

examples.question: An nMOS has W = 1 µm, L = 0.25 µm, tox = 4 nm and an overlap of Lov = 0.02 µm at each side. Take εox = 3.45×10⁻¹¹ F/m. Find Cox in fF/µm², the gate area capacitance, the overlap capacitance per side, Cgs and Cgd in saturation, the total gate capacitance in saturation, and Cgs in cutoff.
steps: Step 1: Cox = εox / tox = 3.45×10⁻¹¹ / 4×10⁻⁹ = 8.625×10⁻³ F/m². Since 1 F/m² = 1000 fF/µm², Cox = 8.625 fF/µm² ≈ 8.63 fF/µm².
Step 2: Gate area capacitance = CoxWL = 8.625 × 1 × 0.25 = 2.156 fF ≈ 2.16 fF.
Step 3: Overlap per side = Cov = Cox W Lov = 8.625 × 1 × 0.02 = 0.1725 fF ≈ 0.17 fF.
Step 4: In saturation, Cgs = ⅔ × area + Cov = 1.4375 + 0.1725 = 1.610 fF ≈ 1.61 fF. Cgd = Cov = 0.17 fF.
Step 5: Total gate capacitance in saturation = Cgs + Cgd = 1.610 + 0.1725 = 1.7825 fF ≈ 1.78 fF.
Step 6: In cutoff, the channel is absent, so Cgs = Cgd = Cov = 0.17 fF. The area capacitance appears from gate to bulk: Cgb ≈ 2.16 fF.
examples.answer: Cox ≈ 8.63 fF/µm², gate area ≈ 2.16 fF, overlap ≈ 0.17 fF per side, saturation Cgs ≈ 1.61 fF and Cgd ≈ 0.17 fF, total gate capacitance ≈ 1.78 fF, and cutoff Cgs ≈ 0.17 fF.

tox = 4e-9
W = 1.0
L = 0.25
Lov = 0.02
cox = eps / tox * 1e3
area = cox * W * L
ov = cox * W * Lov
cgs_sat = (2/3) * area + ov
cgd_sat = ov
total = cgs_sat + cgd_sat

def r(x):
    return round(x + 1e-12, 2)
print(f"{r(cox):.2f}")
print(f"{r(area):.2f}")
print(f"{r(ov):.2f}")

traps: Using CoxWL as the gate capacitance in every region. In saturation Cgs is about ⅔CoxWL plus overlap, and Cgd is only overlap.
Ignoring overlap capacitance. For short L, CGSO·W and CGDO·W can dominate the gate capacitance.
Writing the junction capacitance as a fixed number. It falls with reverse voltage as Cj0/(1 + V/VB)^m.
Mixing units: Cox in F/m² with W and L in µm gives the wrong scale. Convert Cox to fF/µm² or use metres throughout.
Treating gate resistance as one lump. A wide gate is an RC ladder; one resistor underestimates the charging delay.

quiz.q: What does Cox represent, and what are its units?
quiz.a: Cox is the gate oxide capacitance per unit area, Cox = εox/tox. Its SI unit is F/m²; a convenient unit is fF/µm².

quiz.q: Why is Cgd only the overlap capacitance in saturation?
quiz.a: The channel is pinched off near the drain, so the gate charge is not connected to the drain through inversion charge. Only the lateral overlap under the gate remains as gate-drain capacitance.

quiz.q: A transistor has CoxWL = 4 fF and Cov = 0.2 fF per side. Find Cgs and Cgd in saturation.
quiz.a: In saturation, Cgs = ⅔ × 4 + 0.2 = 2.667 + 0.2 = 2.87 fF. Cgd = Cov = 0.2 fF.

quiz.q: Why can a short-channel device have Cgs larger than the simple ⅔CoxWL estimate?
quiz.a: The overlap and fringing capacitances are added to the channel term. When L is short, Cov can be a large fraction of CoxWL. The simple ⅔ fraction ignores these extra fields.

quiz.q: Name the SPICE parameters for overlap capacitance and junction capacitance.
quiz.a: Overlap: CGSO, CGDO and CGBO per unit width. Junction: CJ per unit area, CJSW per unit perimeter, plus Cj0, VB and m in the bias equation.

quiz.q: Why is the source-bulk junction capacitance voltage dependent?
quiz.a: The junction depletion width changes with reverse bias. A larger reverse voltage widens the depletion region and reduces the capacitance, as Cj = Cj0/(1 + V/VB)^m.

quiz.q: A poly gate is 1 µm wide and has sheet resistance 10 Ω/square. Why is a single resistor a poor model?
quiz.a: The gate contact charges the channel along the width, so the resistance and gate capacitance are distributed. The RC ladder gives a slower response than one lumped resistor with the same total values.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, parasitic extraction tools compute these capacitances from layout and feed them to SPICE. BSIM models include bias-dependent overlap and junction terms, and FinFETs add three-dimensional fringing. Search for parasitic extraction, BSIM-CMG capacitance model, and RC ladder gate resistance.
